analysis.title: "Not Enough Fear": Fund Managers Dump Tech At Fastest Pace Since 2006, Beg Hyperscalers To Stop Spending... And Still Have No Cash
key_insights: BofA's November Fund Manager Survey (193 panellists, $526B AUM, Nov 6-12) shows the net overweight in tech fell to 12% from 37% in one month. The 25-point cut is the largest since June 2006.
Average cash fell to 3.6% from 3.9%, which is 1.9 standard deviations below its long-term average. Under BofA's Cash Rule, a reading at or below 4.0% is a contrarian sell signal for global stocks.

Hartnett concludes the Nov FMS does not show enough investor fear to buy and stays tactically risk-off. Boom expectations fell to 41% from 47% while cash stayed below 3.7%, which was his test for 'still not enough fear'.

A record net 38% of fund managers say companies are overinvesting. Only 16% want companies to increase capex, the lowest since May 2020, versus 34% in January. 42% want balance sheet improvement and 33% want cash returned to shareholders.
52% expect an AI hyperscaler to announce a capex cut in the next six months, up from 30% in October. In September, 79% said no hyperscaler would cut AI capex this year.
The top two tail risks are both AI: 'AI bubble' (34%) and 'AI hyperscaler credit event' (31%), together 65%. October's top risk, a disorderly rise in bond yields, fell to 13%.
The most likely source of a systemic credit event is AI hyperscaler bonds (38%), followed by private credit (30%).
'Long global semiconductors' is still the most crowded trade but at 39%, less than half July's record 82%. 'Short China stocks' (14%) is second, ahead of 'long Mag 7' (12%).
The base case is a soft landing (50%) for the first time since June, versus no landing (42%). Only 3% expect a hard landing. The share expecting a 'boom' fell to 41% from 47%.

A net 32% expect lower global CPI in 12 months, the weakest reading since October 2024, even though CPI has run hot for a third straight month, producer prices are at a four-year high and the market prices Fed hikes in December, January and March.

The bond underweight was cut 13 points to a net 23%, the smallest since November 2025. Managers say the 10-year yield needs to reach a weighted average of 5.8% for them to go overweight bonds. The 10-year is at 5.1% and the survey's end-2027 target is 4.9%.

The combined allocation to consumer discretionary and staples had its biggest one-month jump since June 2006. Managers remain net 20% underweight discretionary and net 18% underweight staples, versus 34% and 32% a month earlier.

Healthcare is the favored sector (net 34% overweight, from 23%). Energy was cut (net 12% underweight, from 4%). Japan was cut to neutral. A record net 23% say gold is undervalued, with gold at $3,868.

Net equity overweight is 41%, down 3 points from October. US equity allocation rose to a net 13% from 11%. BofA's Bull & Bear Indicator is at 7.4, versus 9.5 in September and the sub-2 reading that triggers a contrarian buy.
Hartnett's contrarian pair trades from the survey: long cash/gold vs short stocks, long consumer vs short health care, long REITs vs short banks, long energy vs short industrials.

2027 views: best asset classes are international stocks (36%), US stocks (24%) and gold (17%). Best currency is the yen (42%). Average end-2027 targets are S&P 500 7,926, gold $4,341, 10-year yield 4.9%, EURUSD 1.12.

The article argues the move is rotation rather than capitulation. It expects a bounce in dumped tech names but bets cash needs to rise nearer 5% before a real bottom, citing Nvidia's first quarter report without Jensen Huang, dealers the most short gamma since 2019 and a Fed hiking.

Context cited: the survey window opened the morning after the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4% and the SOX fell 12%, and closed on the day Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO. Goldman's prime brokerage recorded the biggest weekly cut in hedge fund gross leverage since March 2020 and a record low tech long/short ratio.

market_movers.rationale: The article flags Nvidia reporting its first quarter without Jensen Huang as CEO, after the SOX fell 12% in one day, as a risk to the tech bounce.

sector_views.rationale: FMS net overweight in tech fell to 12% from 37%, the largest cut since June 2006. BofA history suggests best entry points come when tech is cut to underweight, which has not happened yet.
Net 34% overweight, up from 23%, the new favorite sector in the survey.
Net 12% underweight, from 4% a month earlier.
Net 20% underweight, down from 34%, a short-covering move.

earnings_insights: Goldman's 2027 outlook, as cited, has S&P 500 earnings growth falling to 11% next year from 36% as capex peaks and depreciation rises (forecast).
Nvidia is described as about to report its first quarter without Jensen Huang as CEO (upcoming report, no estimate given).

macro_indicators.interpretation: Weakest inflation expectation reading since October 2024 despite CPI running hot for a third straight month. This is a survey result, not an economic print.
Fund managers say they need about 5.8% to move from stocks to bonds, while the survey's end-2027 target is 4.9%.
Managers expect yields to fall while waiting for a rise to 5.8% before buying bonds.
Gold broke below $4,000, down from about $5,000 in February. A record net 23% of managers call it undervalued.
Recession risk is largely ignored in positioning.
Just under 5% above current levels. Only 1% see it finishing below 6,500.

vol_and_positioning: Average FMS cash is 3.6%, down from 3.9% and 1.9 standard deviations below its long-term average. BofA's Cash Rule (4.0% or lower) is a contrarian sell signal for global stocks. The median four-week return after such signals since 2011 is -1%, the worst -29%.
BofA's broadest FMS sentiment gauge fell to 6.3 from 6.4. The Bull & Bear Indicator is 7.4, versus 9.5 in September.
Net tech positioning is half a standard deviation below its long-term average. Goldman's tech long/short ratio hit a record low.

A net 16% expect low momentum to beat high momentum, versus a net 36% expecting the opposite in January. A net 71% want high-quality earnings over low-quality.
Net equity overweight is 41%. US equity allocation is a net 13%, up from 11%.

tension_points.bull_case: Tech has been cut harder than at any point in two decades and BofA history shows the best entries come when tech is cut to underweight, which argues for a bounce. Hartnett names tech credit scare fading as the bull risk.
tension_points.bear_case: Cash is only 3.6%, net equity overweight is 41% and only 3% expect a hard landing, so the move is rotation rather than capitulation. Real bottoms come with cash near 5%.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Cash rising above 4.2% with a big drop in boom expectations would signal sentiment is no longer a headwind. The Bull & Bear Indicator falling below 2 triggers BofA's contrarian buy.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscalers have kept spending despite investor pressure, and a fading of tech credit concerns is the stated bull risk.
tension_points.bear_case: 52% expect a hyperscaler capex cut within six months and 65% name AI as the top tail risk. AI hyperscaler bonds are the most likely credit event source at 38%.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A hyperscaler announcing a capex cut within six months would confirm the bear case. Tech credit concerns fading is the bull trigger Hartnett names.
